text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- Austria's ruling Social Democrats lost almost five percent of votes in Sunday's municipal elections in the southern province of Carinthia. The far-right Freedom Party gained nearly five percent, while the conservatie People's Party lost more than two percent. The Social Democrats remained the strongest party.
- In a referendum on Sunday, residents of Tyrol's capital Innsbruck voted against launching a bid to host the Winter Olympics in the year 2006.

- Austria's energy industry is badly equipped for the liberalisation of the market, says a new study by international consultants Price Waterhouse. Personnel costs are too high, the market is overcrowded and there is a lack of foreign strategic partners, the study says.
- Conservative People's Party leader Wolfgang Schuessel said he was convinced his party had a chance of winning the next general elections, due in 1999.
- Steelmaker VA Stahl is still searching for a strategic partner.
- Raiffeisen Zentralbank will be the first Austrian bank to open a fully licensed subsidiary in Moscow next month.
- Vice-Chancellor and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel wants the government's report on Austria's future security policy to be completed before the end of the year.
- Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner plans to offer financial support to companies which face higher costs due to an increase in health insurance payments for trainees.
- Die Erste savings bank will have to pay eight billion schillings for the City of Vienna's stake in GiroCredit.
- Conservative party chief Wolfgang Schuessel demands a reform of Austria's tax system by the year 1999, says the reform should primarily benefit families.
- Austrian telecommunications companies criticise a draft liberalisation law for the industry as being too soft on state monopoly Post & Telekom Austria.
- The European Union has demanded Bank Austria must sell some of its stakes in construction companies as a condition for approval of the takeover of rival Creditanstalt.
- Austrian tourists have spent less money abroad in 1996 than a year ago, mostly because of the Italian Lira's appreciation.
